items.text: India's  journey  in  space  exploration  began  in  1962  with  the establishment  of  the  Indian  National  Committee  for  Space Research (INCOSPAR)  under the leadership of Dr. Vikram Sarabhai. What  started  with  modest  rocket  launches  from Thumba  soon evolved  into  one  of  the  world's  most  respected space  programs.  The  formation  of  the  Indian  Space  Research Organisation  (ISRO)  in  1969  marked  a  turning  point,  reflecting India's ambition to harness space technology  for  national development. Over  the  decades,  ISRO  achieved  remarkable milestones  -  from launching the Aryabhata satellite in 1975 to the  Chandrayaan  and  Mangalyaan  missions  that  showcased India's prowess in lunar and interplanetary exploration. However, the  true  transformation  occurred  in  the  21st  century.  With  the successful  launch  of  the Chandrayaan-3 mission in 2023, India became the first nation to land on the Moon's south pole, a feat celebrated globally. The mission highlighted ISRO's cost-effective  innovation  and  technical  expertise.  Meanwhile, projects like Gaganyaan, India's first human spaceflight program, signify  the  country's  leap  toward  manned  missions.  ISRO's collaborations  with  private  space  startups and global agencies are  also  expanding

items.text: In  the  contemporary  era,  the  relationship  between  technology and  human  cognition  has  become  increasingly  intertwined. Digital  tools  have  transformed  how  we  process,  store,  and retrieve information. On one hand, technology enhances efficiency -  allowing instantaneous access to knowledge, fostering global communication, and enabling complex problem-solving. On the other hand, constant digital engagement has raised concerns about attention fragmentation, superficial learning, and declining memory retention. Psychologists argue that reliance on external devices for information storage-commonly termed as 'digital amnesia'-may  erode  our  natural cognitive abilities.  When individuals  delegate  tasks  like  remembering  phone  numbers, dates, or even directions to devices, they strengthen convenience but weaken mental endurance. However, advocates of  digital  integration  claim  that  such  delegation  allows  the human  mind  to  focus  on  higher-order  thinking  rather  than routine recall. They argue that every technological revolution-printing press, calculator, or computer-has similarly redefined  intelligence  rather  than  diminished  it.  The  central challenge,  therefore,  is  not  resisting  technology  but  using  it judiciously-balancing cognitive independence with technological assistance. The future of human intellect will likely depend  on  how  effectively  individuals  cultivate  mindfulness  in an age of mental automation.
